questions.question_text: A 32-year-old man with moderate depression and mild functional impairment is referred for psychological therapy. Which intervention is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Individual CBT is recommended for moderate depression with functional impairment.

questions.question_text: Which of the following elements differentiates empathy from identification?

options.text: Being able to experience the emotion

questions.explanation: The ability to maintain objectivity is crucial in a therapeutic relationship and can differentiate empathy from identification. With identification, psychiatrists experience as well as understand the emotion, which can lead to boundary problems along with physician burnout.

questions.question_text: In the treatment of borderline personality disorder, which of the following does Stage 2 of dialectical behaviour treatment target?

options.text: Maladaptive coping patterns and difficulties with emotional regulation in daily functioning

questions.explanation: Treatment of borderline personality disorder is organized around the level of the disorder, with each level corresponding to one of four stages of treatment with specifi c goals that are targeted towards core defi cits seen in these patients. Stage I: In the fi rst stage of treatment, the therapist seeks to increase behavioural control through helping patients attain basic capacities. This is targeted towards the severe ‘behavioural dyscontrol’ exhibited by the patient. Stage II: The second stage targets ‘quiet desperation’. The intent in this stage is to facilitate emotional experiencing through reducing post-traumatic stress and blocking dissociation. The principal goal of this stage is to block avoidance of emotions and the environmental cues associated with them. In this stage, patients are helped to experience their feelings without avoiding life or experiencing symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder. Stage III: The third stage is targeted towards ‘problematic patterns in living’. The goal of this stage is to achieve ‘ordinary happiness and unhappiness’ through increasing self-respect and working on problems with relationships and career choices. Stage IV: The fourth and fi nal stage is directed towards ‘incompleteness’. The goal of the last stage is to develop the patient’s capacity for sustained experience of contentment, connection, and freedom. Gabbard GO. Textbook of Psychotherapeutic Treatments in Psychiatry, 1st edn. American Psychiatric Publishing, 2008, p. 736.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which therapies involve ‘strokes’ that people exchange and ‘games’ that people play?
questions.explanation: Transactional analysis developed by Eric Berne in 1960s. According to Berne, transactions are stimuli presented by one person that evoke a corresponding response in another. Berne defi ned psychological ‘games’ as stereotyped and predictable transactions that people learn in childhood and continue to play throughout their lives. Strokes, the basic motivating factors of human behaviour consist of specifi c rewards such as approval and love. All people have three ego states that exist within them: the child (the primitive element), the adult (the reality element), and the parent (an introject of the values of a person’s actual parents). The therapeutic process helps people to understand whether they are functioning in a child, adult or parent mode when interacting with others. It is thought that as patients learn to recognize characteristic games being repeated throughout life, they can ultimately function in the adult mode as much as possible in interpersonal relationships. Sadock BJ and Sadock VA. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry: Behavioral Sciences/clinical Psychiatry, 10th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2007, p. 216. Freeman C and Power M (). Handbook of Evidence-based Psychotherapies: A Guide for Research and Practice, 1st edn. WileyBlackwell 2007, p. 129.

questions.question_text: What does the Q Sort test measure in psychology?
questions.explanation: The Q Sort test is used to study people's subjectivity and viewpoint. It uses factor analysis to understand how people think about an issue and can be used in both clinical and research settings.

questions.question_text: Reciprocal inhibition (Wolpe) is used therapeutically in which treatment approach?

options.text: Systematic desensitization and relaxation therapy for anxiety

correct_answer.text: Systematic desensitization and relaxation therapy for anxiety

questions.explanation: Reciprocal inhibition, described by Wolpe, is based on the principle that if a stimulus with a desired response and a stimulus with an undesired response are presented together repeatedly, the incompatibility leads to reduction in the undesired response. This is used in relaxation therapy for anxiety and systematic desensitization.

questions.question_text: Which therapeutic technique involves imagining a feared situation with maximum intensity to reduce phobic anxiety?
questions.explanation: Implosion therapy (also called implosive therapy) involves having the patient imagine the feared situation with maximum intensity and vividness to reduce phobic anxiety.

questions.question_text: During substance abuse therapy, the use of alcohol or substance signifier in controlled conditions is characteristic of which therapy?
questions.explanation: Cue exposure therapy is a behavioral therapy technique where alcohol or substance cues are presented in controlled conditions to reduce conditioned responses and craving.

questions.question_text: Which family therapy approach improves communication between family members and utilizes an eclectic style?
questions.explanation: Eclectic family therapy draws from multiple approaches to improve communication and family functioning based on individual family needs.

questions.question_text: During substance abuse treatment, people believe that they are helpless, hopeless and powerless
questions.explanation: The 12-step program acknowledges that individuals feel powerless over their addiction and emphasizes surrender to a higher power as part of recovery.

questions.question_text: Enmeshment in family systems theory refers to:

options.text: Lack of autonomy with blurred boundaries

correct_answer.text: Lack of autonomy with blurred boundaries

questions.explanation: Enmeshment is a family systems concept describing relationships with excessively diffused boundaries, little autonomy, and excessive interdependence.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which forms of grief treatment treats unresolved grief as a form of phobic avoidance?
questions.explanation: Some individuals with abnormal grief reaction may be avoiding reminders of their grief, leading to unresolved emotions. Addressing these issues by encouragement may not be suffi cient and a behavioural approach may be needed in some cases. The approach commonly used is known as guided mourning. This treats unresolved grief in a way similar to other forms of phobic avoidance by exposure to the avoided situation. Thus guided mourning involves intense reliving of avoided painful memories and feelings associated with bereavement. During treatment, patients are exposed to avoided painful memories or situations related to the loss of their loved one – both in imagination and in real life. Clark A. Working with grieving adults. Advances in Psychiatric Treatment 2004; 10: 164–170.

questions.question_text: During substance abuse treatment, people believe they are helpless, hopeless, and powerless. What program is this?
questions.explanation: The 12-step program emphasizes acceptance of powerlessness and the need for a higher power in recovery from addiction.

questions.question_text: In substance abuse therapy, cue exposure involves exposure to alcohol or substance signifiers under which type of treatment?
questions.explanation: Cue exposure therapy is a behavioral technique where patients are exposed to conditioned substance cues in controlled conditions to reduce conditioned responses.

questions.question_text: Which type of therapy asks patients to direct their attention to specific body area while thinking certain phrases reflecting a relaxed state, progressing through various themes including cardiac regulation and breathing adjustment?
questions.explanation: Autogenic training can help with relaxation by having the patient direct attention to specific body areas and think phrases to help them relax (i.e., My forehead is cool.).

questions.question_text: During substance abuse therapy, alcohol or substance signifier is used in controlled conditions. What therapy is this?
questions.explanation: Cue exposure therapy involves presenting substance-related cues in controlled environments to reduce conditioned cravings and relapse.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is not a goal of family treatment?

options.text: Establishing clarity about tasks and responsibilities of family members
Reducing tension and disagreements between family members
Decreasing distress in the member considered to be the individual

questions.explanation: Family therapy is mostly employed in child psychiatry settings, when problems have usually been identifi ed in a child’s behaviour, which has led the family to seek help. The aim of family therapy is to improve family functioning and so help the identifi ed patient. The goals of family therapy include (1) improved communications; (2) improved autonomy for each member; (3) improved agreement about roles; (4) reduced confl ict; (5) reduced distress in the member who is the patient. Family therapy developed from Ackerman’s work on psychodynamics of family and Bateson’s work on communication. Ackerman’s work led to the development of psychodynamic methods of treatment, while Bateson’s work led to the system’s approach. Minuchin developed further the system’s approach in the USA to form the structural family therapy method. Gelder M, Harrison P, and Cowen P. Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, 5th edn. Oxford University Press, 2006, p. 611.

questions.question_text: In the ENRICHD study evaluating CBT for depression after myocardial infarction, what was the primary outcome regarding survival?

options.text: CBT had modest effects on depression and did not improve survival
CBT improved survival but not depression scores

correct_answer.text: CBT had modest effects on depression and did not improve survival

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that in the primary analyses, the ENRICHD intervention had only modest effects on depression and neither ENRICHD nor MIND-IT improved survival. Options A and D overstate the benefits, and option C is unrealistic.

questions.question_text: Paradoxical injunctions are a technique used in which family therapy approach?
questions.explanation: Paradoxical interventions and injunctions are characteristic techniques of systemic/strategic family therapy approaches.

questions.question_text: Nick has been presenting with a diagnosis of major depression. His GP is considering referring Nick for psychodynamic psychotherapy. According to the GP, Nick has certain qualities he thinks are significant for a good clinical outlook in psychodynamic psychotherapy. Which of the qualities shown by Nick has been shown NOT to predict good response in psychodynamic psychotherapy?

options.text: High levels of personality pathology or severe personality traits

questions.explanation: Most psychotherapists consider certain qualities in their patients as prerequisites for engaging in psychodynamic psychotherapy. These include psychological mindedness: curiosity about oneself and the capacity for self-scrutiny. Those who are unable to articulate and comprehend their inner thoughts and feelings cannot negotiate with the fundamental analytical words and their meanings. The inability to examine one’s own motivations and behaviours precludes benefi ts from the analytical method. Introspectiveness: the person should be able to experience and learn from intense affects or confl icts without acting them out. The person should be able to form reasonable object relationships, usually the capacity to form and maintain, as well as to detach from, a trusting object relationship is essential. High motivation: the patient needs a strong motivation to persevere, in light of the rigors of intense and lengthy treatment. The desire for health and self-understanding must surpass the neurotic need for unhappiness. The person should be able to tolerate frustration and therapeutic regression. Sadock BJ and Sadock VA. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry: Behavioral Sciences/clinical Psychiatry, 10th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2007, p. 926. Tasman A, Maj M, First MB, et al. Psychiatry, 3rd edn. WileyBlackwell, 2008, p. 1862.

questions.question_text: Rachel is a 35-year-old woman who was recently involved in a life- threatening road traffi c accident. She developed symptoms suggestive of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) over a period of a month following the accident. The symptoms interfered with her daily activities. She refused to drive to work and started missing her work. She also stopped taking her children to the nursery. According to NICE guidelines, what treatment is recommended?

options.text: Monitoring of symptoms without active intervention for the first three months

questions.explanation: The NICE recommends ‘Watchful waiting’ when symptoms are mild and have been present for less than 4 weeks after the trauma, with a follow-up contact within 1 month. NICE specifi cally asks therapists and clinicians not to routinely offer brief, single-session interventions (debriefi ng) that focus on the traumatic incident to that individual alone. Where symptoms are present for less than 3 months (as in the case with Rachel), NICE specifi cally recommends trauma-focused CBT (usually on an individual outpatient basis. Trauma-focused CBT is also recommended for people with ‘severe’ symptoms or ‘severe’ PTSD within 1 month. NICE recommends 8–12 weekly sessions of trauma-focused CBT, each session delivered by the same person and lasting around 90 minutes during which trauma is discussed. NICE advises against the use of non-directed therapies such as relaxation training. Where symptoms are milder and have lasted for more than 3 months, NICE recommends either trauma-focused CBT or EMDR. In addition to psychological treatments, NICE also recommends specifi c pharmacological interventions. NICE. Clinical Guideline 26: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD): the management of PTSD in adults and children in primary and secondary care. www.nice.org.uk/CG026NICEguideline

questions.question_text: Exposing a patient to alcohol and drug misuse stimuli without actually taking substances represents which therapeutic approach?
questions.explanation: Behavioral therapy involving exposure to drug and alcohol cues without substance use helps reduce cue-induced cravings through extinction.

questions.question_text: Reflecting on how intended outcomes are affected by current behaviors is characteristic of which therapy
questions.explanation: Motivational interviewing is a counseling method that helps resolve ambivalent feelings about behavior change by exploring how current behaviors affect desired outcomes. It is practical, empathetic, and short-term, based on helping clients find internal motivation.

questions.question_text: In substance abuse therapy, which approach uses alcohol or substance signifiers in controlled conditions to reduce cravings?
questions.explanation: Cue therapy, also known as cue exposure therapy, uses alcohol or substance signifiers in controlled conditions to help individuals with substance use disorders reduce their cravings and problematic behaviors related to substance abuse.

questions.question_text: Focusing on a detail out of context while ignoring other, more salient features in the situation is called
questions.explanation: The statement refers to selective abstraction, one of the cognitive biases seen in depression. Other cognitive biases include arbitrary inference, drawing a specifi c conclusion in the absence of evidence or when the evidence is contrary to the conclusion; overgeneralization, drawing a conclusion on the basis of one or more isolated incidents; dichotomous thinking, the tendency to classify experience in one of two extreme categories, ignoring more moderate variations; personalization, the tendency to relate external events to oneself; magnifi cation/ minimization,- exaggerating (i.e. catastrophizing) or belittling the signifi cance or magnitude of an event. Gabbard GO. Textbook of Psychotherapeutic Treatments in Psychiatry, 1st edn. American Psychiatric Publishing, 2008, p. 173.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is considered to be the most significant therapeutic factor in group psychotherapy?

options.text: Expression of emotion and cathartic release of tensions

questions.explanation: Cohesion is the sense that the group is working together towards a common goal. This is believed to be the most important factor related to positive therapeutic effects. Group cohesion has been likened to the therapeutic alliance in dyadic treatment. In dynamic therapies, specifi c and non-specifi c elements contribute to therapeutic change. In groups, the presence of other people adds to factors present in all dyadic healing relationships. Non-specifi c factors are embedded in the relationships established through a consistent, accepting, non-judgemental, and supportive environment. These are all elements of a cohesive group. Groups provide a corrective emotional experience in which patients experience others (including the therapist) responding to them differently from those in their past. Members share their stories (catharsis) and feel less isolated when others have shared similar stories (universalization); they have opportunities to be helpful to others through both cognitive understanding and emotional linking (imparting information, providing feedback, and altruism). They also see others improve, which conveys hope. These elements contribute to the sense of collaboration and a willingness to adopt norms (i.e. discuss feelings about the interactions in the meeting) that further members’ sense of effi cacy and belonging. They contribute to an experience of support and acceptance, which may be suffi cient therapeutic gain for a number of patients. Fight/fl ight, pairing, and dependency are Bion’s basic group assumptions that lead to a negative therapeutic effect. Tasman A, Maj M, First MB, et al. Psychiatry, 3rd edn. WileyBlackwell, 2007, p. 1908.

questions.question_text: Covert sensitisation is best used in the treatment of which of the following

options.text: A diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder
A diagnosis of major depressive disorder

questions.explanation: Covert sensitisation is a variant of aversive conditioning wherein images (e.g. of drinking situations) is paired with imaginary aversive stimuli (e.g. a scene of a person vomiting all over the place, or a scene of a person dying of alcohol-induced liver damage). It is called covert because neither the undesirable stimulus nor the aversive stimulus is actually presented except in the imagination. Sensitization refers to the intention to build up an avoidance response to the undesirable stimulus. This is based on aversion therapy. Freeman C and Power M. Handbook of Evidence-based Psychotherapies: A Guide for Research and Practice, 1st edn. WileyBlackwell, 2007, p. 70.

questions.question_text: Detouring in family systems theory refers to:

options.text: Redirecting family conflict through a child

correct_answer.text: Redirecting family conflict through a child

questions.explanation: Detouring is a family dynamic where parents redirect their marital conflict through a child, often by coalitioning with the child against the other parent.

questions.question_text: A shy 26yearold female patient has never been in a romantic relationship. After 5 months of psychodynamic treatment, she begins to struggle with strong positive feelings toward her male therapist, which she finds hard to accept. This occurs at the same time she is beginning to date someone from work. Her relationship with her colleague is likely an example of:
questions.explanation: Sometimes patients are not aware of their repressed feelings and express them as an action— as this patient is doing with her colleague. The action is repeated in an unconscious manner. For the therapist it is important to try to understand what is being communicated. Transference is generally defined as the set of expectations, beliefs, and emotional responses that a patient brings to the patient– doctor relationship, which are not necessarily based on who the doctor is or how the doctor acts in reality but, rather, on repeated experiences the patient has had with other important authority figures throughout life.

questions.question_text: Lisa is a 35-year-old lady, presenting with a diagnosis of depression. She has been referred by her psychiatrist for psychodynamic psychotherapy. According to her therapist, Lisa has the ability to conceive of her own mental state as explanations of her behaviour. This phenomenon is called
questions.explanation: The capacity for mentalizing grows out of attachment theory and refers to a person’s ability to conceive of his or her own and others’ mental states as explanations of behaviour. Hence, it is related to psychological mindedness. The psychodynamic clinician assesses the ability of a patient to see that his or her behaviour grows out of a set of beliefs, feelings, and perspectives that are not necessarily the same as others’. Like empathy, mentalizing requires a capacity to sense what is going on in another’s mind and respond accordingly. This capacity to be sensitive to what others are feeling and to know that one’s internal states contribute to one’s behaviour augurs well for a more exploratory or interpretative approach in dynamic psychotherapy. Gabbard GO. Textbook of Psychotherapeutic Treatments in Psychiatry,1st edn. American Psychiatric Publishing, 2008, p 29.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which indicates suffi cient psychological mindedness in Lisa?

options.text: She is capable of describing her feelings without excessive defensive reactions
She demonstrates insight into the connections between past experiences and current patterns
She recognizes the influence of unconscious motivations on her behavior
She does not have poor self-esteem
She can engage in self-reflection and examine her own mental processes

correct_answer.text: She does not have poor self-esteem

questions.explanation: According to Nina Coltart, during psychotherapy, a therapist is exercising his/her skills and psychological mindedness to explore the patient’s psyche. If the patient is also psychologically minded, the prospects of treatment success are thought to be greatly increased. Whether a patient is psychologically minded depends on a number of characters. They include: 1. The capacity to give a history that deepens, acquires more coherence, and becomes texturally more substantial as it goes on. 2. The capacity to give such a history without needing too much prompting, and a history which gives the listener an increasing awareness that the patient feels currently related in him/herself, to his/her own story. 3. The capacity to bring up memories with appropriate affects. 4. Some awareness in the patient that he has an unconscious mental life. 5. Some capacity to step back, if only momentarily, from self-experience, and to observe it refl ectively. 6. The capacity, or more strongly a wish, to accept and handle increased responsibility for the self. 7. The capacity to imagine and dream and use metaphors. 8. Some capacity for achievement, and some realistic self-esteem. Coltart N. The assessment of psychological-mindedness in the diagnostic interview. British Journal of Psychiatry 1988; 153: 819–820. Naismith J and Grant S. Seminars in the Psychotherapies. Gaskell, 2007, p. 8.

questions.question_text: The COMPASS Pathways Phase 2b trial (2021) of psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression tested three doses. Which finding most accurately reflects the trial's primary result?

options.text: Trial terminated due to adverse events

questions.explanation: The COMPASS Pathways Phase 2b randomised controlled trial (n=233, published NEJM Evidence 2022) compared single doses of psilocybin (1mg, 10mg, 25mg) for treatment-resistant depression. Key findings: (1) the 25mg dose produced a significantly greater reduction in MADRS score at week 3 compared with the 1mg control dose (primary endpoint, p<0.001); (2) the 10mg dose did not reach statistical significance vs 1mg; (3) the effect was not sustained without support — response rates declined by week 12 in many patients; (4) the 25mg group had more adverse events, including a dose-dependent increase in suicidal ideation/self-injury signals in the first few weeks, requiring careful monitoring; (5) the most common adverse events were headache, nausea, and dizziness; no fatalities. This trial established proof of concept for psilocybin in TRD at the 25mg dose and informed subsequent Phase 3 design. The 1mg dose served as an 'active placebo' (producing minimal psychedelic effects) to maintain blinding.

questions.question_text: Cue exposure therapy for substance use disorders involves:

options.text: Administering the substance in controlled doses
Exposure to drug cues without allowing consumption to extinguish conditioned responses

correct_answer.text: Exposure to drug cues without allowing consumption to extinguish conditioned responses

questions.explanation: Cue exposure therapy exposes substance-dependent patients to the sight and smell of alcohol or drugs without allowing consumption in an attempt to weaken the conditioned stimulus-unconditioned stimulus link via extinction and attenuate cravings.

questions.question_text: In a therapeutic community, the members tolerate behaviour that may not be accepted anywhere else. This process is called
questions.explanation: Permissiveness is the principle where members tolerate behaviour that they may not accept elsewhere. This is also helped by the members having the opportunity to be helpful to others through both cognitive understanding and emotional linking (imparting information, providing feedback, and altruism). Mutual help is the process by which members support each other and help each other to change. Imitation is the conscious emulation of one’s behaviour following that of another – also called role modelling. Altruism is the process of putting another person’s need ahead of one’s own and in the process learning there is value in giving to others. Gelder M, Harrison P, and Cowen P. Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, 5th edn. Oxford University Press, 2006, p. 608. Sadock BJ and Sadock VA. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry: Behavioral Sciences/clinical Psychiatry, 10th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2007, p. 937.

questions.question_text: A patient expressing, “cabbages to kings” during a therapy session is a good example of which fundamental technique in psychoanalysis?
questions.explanation: Free association is a predominant technique in psychoanalysis. The fundamental rule of free association is for the patient to tell the analysis everything that comes to their mind, the unimportant and nonsensical, and it does not mirror normal conversation.

questions.question_text: A patient with major depression is being considered for interpersonal therapy (IPT). Which of the following is a component of interpersonal therapy?
questions.explanation: IPT focuses on four key areas: grief, role transitions, interpersonal disputes, and interpersonal deficits.

questions.question_text: In substance abuse treatment, a therapeutic approach that addresses beliefs that individuals are helpless, hopeless, and powerless is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: The 12-step program framework addresses beliefs of helplessness, hopelessness, and powerlessness by introducing the concept of surrendering to a higher power and finding support through group participation and spiritual growth.

questions.question_text: Which of the following therapies, used in the treatment of addiction, is explicitly based on Carl Rogers\\\'s client-centred approach and the Transtheoretical Model of Change?
questions.explanation:
Motivational Interviewing (MI), developed by Miller and Rollnick, is explicitly grounded in Carl Rogers\\\'s client-centred therapy and is used in the treatment of substance use disorders. The indexed passages confirm that MI is \\\'in line with Roger\\\'s client centred therapy\\\' and is used with the Transtheoretical Model (Prochaska & DiClemente). 
Cognitive therapy (Option C) was developed by Aaron Beck and does not incorporate Rogers\\\'s method. ACT, DBT, and psychoanalysis are also not described in the passages as combining Rogers and Beck in addiction treatment.

questions.question_text: Which therapeutic approach is explicitly described as drawing on Carl Rogers\' client-centred principles to enhance engagement with behaviour change?
questions.explanation: Motivational interviewing (MI) was developed by Miller and Rollnick explicitly \'in line with Rogers\' client-centred therapy\' and uses core Rogerian principles including empathy, reflective listening, and collaborative non-directive engagement.

questions.question_text: Parent clinical approach training is based on the principles of
questions.explanation: Parent management training was fi rst established as a treatment programme by Gerald Patterson in the 1970s. The programme was based on the principles of learning theory, both operant theories and social learning theories, which teach parents to use positive reinforcers, like stickers, toys, or snacks to increase positive behaviour, while using time out tactics to reduce negative behaviour like temper tantrums. Focus is on one problem behaviour at a time. The parents are taught to observe the problem behaviour – the situations and timings at which it occurs. The frequency of this behaviour is usually charted to look at the progress, while abstinence from the behaviour is positively rewarded and indulgence in the behaviour is rewarded with time outs. Parents are also taught to identify behaviours that are incompatible with the ‘problem’ behaviour – e.g. talking nicely instead of whining. These are called ‘competing’ behaviours – and these are usually rewarded. Consistency in rewarding and punishing is important in this setting. This treatment is usually used in childhood disruptive disorders such as oppositional defi ant disorder or conduct disorder. Shaping and chaining are operant techniques used to induce target behaviours. Approximating ‘da’ and ‘da’ to form the word ‘dada’ – to which the daddy hugs the child (reinforcer) is an example of shaping. Chaining is linking of more complex tasks such as wearing a pull-over shirt – this consists of a number of complex steps. Modelling is a social learning technique where a social behaviour is reinforced by society. For example a student who changes dress to fi t in with a certain group of students has a strong likelihood of being accepted and thus reinforced by that group. Koocher GP, Norcross JC and Hill SS. Psychologists’ Desk Reference. Oxford University Press, 2005, p. 328.

questions.question_text: Reciprocal inhibition is employed in which therapeutic technique?
questions.explanation: Reciprocal inhibition, where incompatible responses (e.g., relaxation and anxiety) cannot occur simultaneously, is the principle underlying systematic desensitization used to treat phobias and anxiety disorders.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is not a step in interpersonal psychotherapy for depression?

options.text: Explaining depression as a treatable medical condition

questions.explanation: Because guilt and low self-esteem are characteristic of depression, patients frequently blame themselves and think of themselves as ‘bad’ when problems arise. Although many depressed patients report these negative cognitions, the therapist does not systematically question and evaluate the automatic negative thoughts. Unlike cognitive therapists, interpersonal therapists neither employ thought records nor weigh the evidence to help patients re-evaluate negative cognitions. Instead, therapists shift blame to the illness, which often provides patients with an immediate feeling of relief. Therapists then capitalize on this transient mood improvement by encouraging patients to take positive steps towards resolving interpersonal problems. Gabbard GO. Textbook of Psychotherapeutic Treatments in Psychiatry, 1st edn. American Psychiatric Publishing, 2008, p. 290.

questions.question_text: During substance abuse therapy, alcohol or substance signifier is used in controlled conditions
questions.explanation: Cue-based therapy uses alcohol or substance-related cues (signifiers) presented in controlled, safe environments to facilitate extinction of conditioned responses and reduce cravings.

questions.question_text: Reciprocal inhibition is employed in:
questions.explanation: Reciprocal inhibition is a fundamental principle of systematic desensitization where a relaxation response is paired with anxiety-provoking stimuli in a graded manner, allowing the relaxation response to inhibit the anxiety response.

questions.question_text: A 23yearold male patient with paranoid personality disorder sees you in a clinic for longterm psychodynamic psychotherapy. You are late for one of the appointments by 5 minutes. The individual becomes visibly angry and accuses you of being unprofessional. What will be a reasonable response to this individual?

options.text: This shows your pattern of seeing me as untrustworthy.
You seem to be testing whether I will set appropriate boundaries.
You’ve been late for several of your sessions. This is my first time being late.
Let's explore what this might mean in the context of your experience.

correct_answer.text: You’ve been late for several of your sessions. This is my first time being late.

questions.explanation: Several synthetic and semisynthetic opioids are not detected on routine urine toxicology screening. For instance, fentanyl, buprenorphine, and methadone require assays for these substances in particular given structural differences relative to naturally occurring opioids (i.e., opiates), including morphine and codeine. Of note, all agents that activate mu receptors are known as opioids (literally, “resembling opiates”), and agonists that are structurally related to compounds derived from opium poppy are opiates proper. The DSM5 uses the more encompassing term opioid, as in “opioid use disorder” and “opioid withdrawal.”

questions.question_text: A 28-year-old woman with moderate PMDD symptoms desires non-pharmacological management. According to the source, which interventions are appropriate for this severity level?

options.text: Lifestyle changes, CBT, exercise, or dietary regulation

correct_answer.text: Lifestyle changes, CBT, exercise, or dietary regulation

questions.explanation: Mild symptoms can be managed by making lifestyle changes, CBT, exercise or dietary regulation. For severe PMDD/PMS, and in those with severe mood symptoms, drug therapy is warranted. Since the patient has moderate (not mild or severe) symptoms, non-pharmacological approaches are reasonable first-line options. Options A, C, D, and E represent pharmacological or overly intensive interventions not indicated for moderate severity. ---

questions.question_text: Cognitive treatment aims to modify the schemas that perpetuate depression or anxiety. Which of the following is least likely with respect to schemas?

options.text: Schemas act as cognitive frameworks that filter and interpret incoming information
Schemas are behaviours representative of the individual’s presenting problem
Conditional assumptions and rules can operate as dysfunctional schemas
Schemas represent fundamental beliefs and assumptions about the self
Not all schemas are pathological or contribute to psychological distress

correct_answer.text: Schemas are behaviours representative of the individual’s presenting problem

questions.explanation: Schemas determine our perceptions, assimilations, and actions upon the externally received information. These are developed through early experiences in childhood and formative infl uences thereafter. According to Beck, these are deeper cognitive structures than the negative automatic thoughts that are readily observable in clients undergoing cognitive behavioural therapy. Everyone interacts with the external world by utilizing his/her set of schemas. Most of these are simple schemas that do not contribute to any psychopathology. So schemas are conditional rules (‘if–then statements’) while the others are core beliefs about oneself (‘I am good-looking’, ‘I cannot write a poem’, etc). Clients requiring CBT often have a cluster of maladaptive schemas that perpetuate depression or anxiety state. Kaplan HI. Kaplan and Sadock’s Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry, 8th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2004. p. 2516.

questions.question_text: A 29-year-old woman with moderate PMDD asks about non-pharmacological options before starting SSRIs. Which evidence-based approach is supported?

options.text: Lifestyle changes alone reliably control severe PMDD
CBT, exercise, and dietary modifications are recommended for mild to moderate symptoms, with severe cases requiring pharmacotherapy
Medication is always required regardless of severity

correct_answer.text: CBT, exercise, and dietary modifications are recommended for mild to moderate symptoms, with severe cases requiring pharmacotherapy

questions.explanation: Mild symptoms can be managed by making lifestyle changes, CBT, exercise or dietary regulation. For severe PMDD/PMS, and in those with severe mood symptoms, drug therapy is warranted. This 2-step reasoning connects symptom severity to treatment intensity, suggesting non-pharmacological approaches for milder presentations.

questions.question_text: Which scenario would make a patient a good candidate for psychoanalysis?

options.text: A diagnosis of a new medical condition
Possessing an urgent need for symptom relief

questions.explanation: Good candidates for psychoanalysis must truly wish to understand themselves and not need urgent symptom relief. Being able to withstand frustration and anxiety without acting out are important characteristics to possess in order for psychoanalysis to be successful.

questions.question_text: After several weeks of weekly psychotherapy for recurrent depression and failed relationships, a individual exclaims to the therapist, “You just expect me to trust you when you never reveal a single thing about yourself. I don’t know anything about you as a person, not even what kind of training you had, how long you have been practicing, and what kind of success, if any, you have 314 • PsyChiatRy had with individuals like me!” How should the therapist respond first?

options.text: Provide facts about his or her credentials.
Explain that selfdisclosure is usually not helpful in psychotherapy.
Confront the individual’s aggressive devaluation of the therapist.
Empathize with the individual’s fears of trust and feelings of being at a disadvantage.
Inquire about the individual’s bad experiences with treatment in the past.

correct_answer.text: Empathize with the individual’s fears of trust and feelings of being at a disadvantage.

questions.explanation: Empathy is a way of increasing rapport. An empathic psychiatrist may anticipate what is felt before it is spoken and can often help patients articulate what they are feeling. Nonverbal cues, such as body posture and facial expression, are noted. Patients’ reactions to the psychiatrist can be understood and clarified. Once the therapist empathizes with the patient, it would not be unreasonable to provide facts about credentials, understanding the patient’s need in the context of the therapy.

questions.question_text: What is the principle of reciprocal inhibition in behavior therapy?

options.text: Two opposing emotions cannot coexist at the same time

correct_answer.text: Two opposing emotions cannot coexist at the same time

questions.explanation: Reciprocal inhibition is the principle that two opposing emotions cannot coexist; it underlies systematic desensitization which uses graded exposure and prevents the anxiety response.

questions.question_text: Which treatment approach for panic disorder is described as both an alternative and an augmentation to pharmacotherapy?
questions.explanation: Cognitive behavioural psychotherapy is described as both an alternative or an augmentation to psychopharmacological approaches in panic disorder. It helps modify cognitive distortions about the catastrophic meaning of panic symptoms, and through graduated exposure techniques, diminishes phobic avoidance behaviours. This dual role — as standalone treatment or combination with medication — reflects the evidence that psychotherapy for anxiety disorders can sometimes be as effective as or more effective than pharmacotherapy alone.

questions.question_text: The therapeutic work of interpersonal psychotherapy is organized around central interpersonal problem areas in the individual’s life. Which of the following situations are possible problem areas in a case of acute depression?
questions.explanation: In acute treatment for depression with IPT, the problem areas can be classifi ed as role transitions (associated with stressful life events), grief, role disputes (e.g. in marriage), or interpersonal defi cits (lack of social support). Although specifi c stressful experiences are relevant to other IPT problem areas in the broadest sense, adjusting to stress and change in the social context requires a role transition. This might be the case in depression following the birth of a child, retirement, medical illness, divorce, etc. According to IPT, bereavement is thought to be a potential precursor of clinical depression. Development of clinical depression following a death is evidence that the normal grief process did not take place and that the individual has had an abnormal grief reaction. In such cases the work of IPT is to help the patient experience the normal grief process. A role dispute can occur in any important relationship especially the patient’s relationship with his or her spouse or signifi cant other. In interpersonal defi cits, the patient’s primary problem is seen as a paucity of social connections. Relationships buffer the individual against stressful life events and are essential to psychological well-being. As such, the primary goal is to enhance the level of social connection through concrete positive changes in the patient’s social activities (e.g. joining a club, taking a class). Attention to social support and a positive social network is also a component of work in the other IPT problem areas. Gabbard GO. Textbook of Psychotherapeutic Treatments in Psychiatry, 1st edn. American Psychiatric Publishing, 2008, p. 275.

questions.question_text: A patient with borderline personality disorder begins dialectical behavior therapy (DBT). What is addressed in the first stage of DBT?
questions.explanation: Stage 1 DBT addresses life-threatening behaviors (self-harm, suicidality) first.

questions.question_text: A female is afraid of heights is shown images of sky-high building and standing on top of building in imagination
questions.explanation: Implosion (imaginal flooding) involves vivid, detailed imaginary exposure to feared stimuli without relaxation techniques, designed to extinguish anxiety through habituation.

questions.question_text: What therapy involves creating an anxiety hierarchy?
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitization involves creating an anxiety hierarchy and gradual exposure to feared stimuli paired with relaxation techniques (reciprocal inhibition).

questions.question_text: Which form of psychotherapy encourages the individual to speak “whatever comes to mind”?
questions.explanation: Psychodynamic psychotherapy is also known as insightoriented or expressive psychotherapy, and its more structured form is known as psychoanalysis. It can be brief or timelimited, but it is usually openended and done in a longterm setting. Sessions usually take place one or two times per week, with the patient being encouraged to speak about “whatever comes to mind.” The goal of psychodynamic psychotherapy is to recognize, interpret, and work through unconscious thoughts and urges that are maladaptive to develop more mature defense mechanisms.

questions.question_text: According to the source, which psychological or behavioral intervention has been most rigorously evaluated for reducing depression and mortality in patients with coronary artery disease?

options.text: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) through multiple trials
No psychological interventions have been evaluated

correct_answer.text: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) through multiple trials

questions.explanation: The source cites multiple RCTs specifically evaluating different interventions (ENRICHD for CBT, MIND-IT, CREATE for interpersonal therapy, COPES for problem-solving, and Women's Hearts Study for CBT-based stress management), indicating CBT and related behavioral approaches have been most systematically evaluated. While the trials showed modest effects, they represent the most rigorous evaluation of behavioral interventions in this population.

questions.question_text: Which therapeutic approach is most appropriate for alcohol addiction?
questions.explanation: Cue exposure therapy (cue therapy) is a psychological treatment used to help individuals with substance use disorders reduce cravings and problematic behaviors by identifying and managing specific cues or triggers that lead to substance cravings and use. This is particularly effective for addiction.

questions.question_text: A 31-year-old patient presents 2 weeks after a car accident. They report anxiety symptoms and are unable to get into cars. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.explanation: At 2 weeks post-trauma, symptoms may resolve spontaneously. Active monitoring/watchful waiting is appropriate before diagnosing PTSD (requires 1 month of symptoms).

questions.question_text: In a family treatment session, the mother is asked to comment on the relationship between her husband and their eldest son. After this, the family members are asked to comment on the mother’s response. This method is called
questions.explanation: Circular questioning is often used in family therapy as part of assessment. The purpose is to discover and clarify confused or confl icting views among the members of the family. Following this, a hypothesis is constructed about family functioning, which is then presented to the family, who should consider it between sessions. The family may be asked to try to behave in new ways. Paradoxical injunctions are used in couples therapy and family therapy. They are provocative statements designed to elicit a benefi cial counter-response that the couple have previously resisted. Very often, this will include a prescription of the ‘unwanted symptom’, which the couple realize and try to give reasons why this is acceptable to the couple. Socratic questioning is a technique used in cognitive therapy. Role reversal is a technique in couples therapy which helps one partner to understand the point of view and experience of the other. Gelder M, Harrison P, and Cowen P. Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, 5th edn. Oxford University Press, 2006, p. 612.

questions.question_text: What does behavioral activation primarily target?
questions.explanation: Behavioral activation targets avoidance and withdrawal by scheduling pleasurable and meaningful activities. It is particularly effective for depression.

questions.question_text: Which therapeutic approach uses conditioned responses and controlled exposure to substance-related cues in alcohol rehabilitation?
questions.explanation: Cue exposure therapy uses controlled presentation of alcohol or substance cues to establish conditioned responses and reduce craving through repeated exposure in the absence of reinforcement, operating through principles of behavioral conditioning.
