questions.explanation: Circular questioning is often used in family therapy as part of assessment. The purpose is to discover and clarify confused or confl icting views among the members of the family. Following this, a hypothesis is constructed about family functioning, which is then presented to the family, who should consider it between sessions. The family may be asked to try to behave in new ways. Paradoxical injunctions are used in couples therapy and family therapy. They are provocative statements designed to elicit a benefi cial counter-response that the couple have previously resisted. Very often, this will include a prescription of the ‘unwanted symptom’, which the couple realize and try to give reasons why this is acceptable to the couple. Socratic questioning is a technique used in cognitive therapy. Role reversal is a technique in couples therapy which helps one partner to understand the point of view and experience of the other. Gelder M, Harrison P, and Cowen P. Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, 5th edn. Oxford University Press, 2006, p. 612.

questions.question_text: How often can periodic booster sessions of exposure and response prevention reduce relapse risk in OCD?

options.text: Booster sessions have no effect on relapse
They significantly reduce relapse risk and provide more durable remission than pharmacotherapy alone
They are only effective in combination with antipsychotics
They are contraindicated after SSRI response

correct_answer.text: They significantly reduce relapse risk and provide more durable remission than pharmacotherapy alone

questions.explanation: That Periodic exposure and response prevention 'booster' sessions can reduce the risk of relapse and provide more durable remission than using pharmacotherapy alone, emphasizing their superior durability compared to medication alone.

questions.question_text: Exposure and response prevention in OCD treatment involves which of the following key components?

options.text: Engagement in compulsive rituals to prevent anxiety
Confrontation of anxiety-provoking situations while abstaining from compulsive behaviours
Gradual reduction of feared stimuli over months

correct_answer.text: Confrontation of anxiety-provoking situations while abstaining from compulsive behaviours

questions.explanation: The source explicitly defines exposure and response prevention: Patients are trained to confront (directly or in imagination) anxiety-provoking situations while abstaining from compulsive behaviours in response. Options A and B describe avoidance and safety behaviours, which are therapeutic targets, not treatments. ---

questions.question_text: Which therapeutic approach is particularly useful for alcohol addiction by managing triggers
questions.explanation: Cue exposure therapy (cue therapy) focuses on identifying and managing specific cues or triggers that lead to substance cravings and use. This approach is particularly effective in addiction treatment by helping individuals reduce responses to environmental triggers.

questions.question_text: Brief psychodynamic psychotherapy has been shown NOT to be of benefi t in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Inclusion criteria for brief psychodynamic psychotherapy diagnoses: depression, mild to moderate; anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, social, panic; somatoform disorders; eating disorders; opiate dependence;. Patient characteristics include good object relationships (has had at least one relationship); highly motivated, ‘willing’ patient; narrow symptom/problem focus; interpersonal diffi culties. Exclusion criteria for brief psychodynamic psychotherapy include a diagnosis of severe depression, bipolar disorder, psychosis, suicidality; obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD); severe somatizing disorders; severe eating disorders; poor object relationships; poor motivation; chronic, severe character pathology; diffuse, ill-defi ned symptomatology. Most of the above criteria are derived from a systematic review of psychodynamic psychotherapies by Leichsenring in 2005. Gabbard GO. Textbook of Psychotherapeutic Treatments in Psychiatry, 1st edn. American Psychiatric Publishing, 2008, p. 73. Leichsenring F. (2005). Are psychodynamic and psychoanalytic therapies effective? A review of empirical data. International Journal of Psycho-Analysis 86: 841–868.

questions.question_text: Cue exposure therapy for substance use disorder involves:

options.text: Exposure to the substance without actual use

correct_answer.text: Exposure to the substance without actual use

questions.explanation: Cue exposure therapy is a behavioral approach where patients are exposed to triggers and cues associated with substance use without actually using the substance, helping to extinguish conditioned responses.

questions.question_text: Which intervention primarily targets a patient's attitudes and beliefs to influence the personal construction of the meaning of illness?
questions.explanation: Cognitive-based interventions target the patient’s attitudes and beliefs towards medication to influence the personal construction of the meaning of medication and illness.

questions.question_text: Which psychotherapeutic approach has the most empirical support for the treatment of borderline personality disorder?
questions.explanation: Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) has the most evidence among psychotherapeutic approaches for treatment of borderline personality disorder.

questions.question_text: Jack is a 35-year-old man who perceived his parents as overly authoritarian. His therapist on the other hand, is friendly and non-authoritarian, but at times fi rm and sets defi nite limits. The attitude of his therapist gave Jack the opportunity to identify with a new parent fi gure. This is an example of a process described by Franz Alexander. Which of the following terms best represents this process?
questions.explanation: The therapeutic relationship between therapist and patient gives a therapist an opportunity to display behaviour different from the destructive or unproductive behaviour of a patient’s parent. At times, such experiences seem to neutralize or reverse some effects of the parents’ mistakes. If the patient had overly authoritarian parents, the therapist’s friendly, fl exible, non-judgemental, non-authoritarian, but at times fi rm and limit-setting attitude gives the patient an opportunity to adjust to, be led by, and identify with a new parent fi gure. Franz Alexander described this process as a corrective emotional experience. It draws on elements of both psychoanalysis and psychoanalytic psychotherapy. Sadock BJ and Sadock VA. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry: Behavioral Sciences/clinical Psychiatry, 10th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2007, p. 931.

questions.question_text: A patient is being treated for a severe phobia of needles. Teaching the patient relaxation strategies, while showing pictures of needles, working toward having them see an actual needle in the office, and then getting a shot at the doctor while experiencing minimal anxiety, is an example of which of the following types of therapies?
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitization is the behavioral principle of counterconditioning, which helps the patient to overcome anxiety by gradually exposing them to the feared situation while they learn to be in a state that inhibits anxiety, called reciprocal inhibition.

questions.question_text: Traps, dilemmas, and snags are techniques characteristically used in
questions.explanation: Cognitive analytical therapy was fi rst developed by Ryle as a brief form of therapy. The therapy is based on the principle that purposeful behaviour activity always follows a sequence. These sequences can be faulty in three ways. Traps are repetitive cycles of behaviour in which the consequence of the behaviour perpetuates it. For example a depressed student is hopeless and stops studying for his exam. He fails the exam, and feels more hopeless and depressed. Dilemmas are false choices or unduly narrowed options. For example, people who fear angry feelings may think they have to choose between placation and aggression. They choose to placate others who then take advantage of them, thus making them even angrier. Snags are the anticipation of highly negative consequences of action such that the action is never carried out and therefore never subject to a reality check. Gelder M, Harrison P, and Cowen P. Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, 5th edn. Oxford University Press, 2006, p. 601.

questions.question_text: Cue therapy is primarily used for treatment of which condition?
questions.explanation: Cue therapy is used to help individuals with alcohol addiction learn to manage responses to environmental cues that trigger addictive behaviors.

questions.question_text: A psychiatrist feels attracted to his individual, and later in the day he realizes that the individual reminds him of the girlfriend he took to prom. This is an example of what?
questions.explanation: Countertransference describes the unconscious response toward a patient based on previous relationships. Transference occurs when a patients’ unconsciously displaces their feelings for significant people in their life onto the treating physician. Recognition of countertransference 26 • PSYCHIATRY is critical to prevent unintended responses toward patients. For example, a physician may choose to not charge a patient for a missed appointment or may give preference in scheduling based on a countertransferential response. BIBlIOgRAPHY Sadock, B.J, & Ruiz, P. (2015). Psychiatric interview, history and mental status Examination. In Kaplan and Sadock’s synopsis of psychiatry: Behavioral sciences, clinical psychiatry (11th ed., p. 194). (J.A.Sadock, Ed.). Philadelphia, PA : Wolters Kluwer.

questions.question_text: In therapy for substance dependence, admission of feeling helpless or powerless is characteristic of
questions.explanation: The 12-step model (used in AA and similar programs) involves acknowledging powerlessness over the substance and seeking higher power support, reflecting themes of helplessness.

questions.question_text: What factor is known to increase the placebo effect?
questions.explanation: Injectable administration tends to enhance placebo effects compared to oral administration, likely due to increased ritual, expectation, and perceived potency associated with injections.

questions.question_text: Circular causality in family systems theory suggests:

options.text: Mutual, reciprocal causality among family members
One member is responsible for all problems
Problems are external to the family

correct_answer.text: Mutual, reciprocal causality among family members

questions.explanation: Circular causality in family systems theory describes mutual, reciprocal causality where family members' behaviors influence each other in circular patterns.

questions.question_text: A key limitation of exposure-based CBT is that:

options.text: It is only effective in patients without comorbid depression
It only applies to phobic avoidance and not to anticipatory anxiety or worry
It requires a minimum of 24 weeks to produce measurable amygdala changes on neuroimaging
Therapeutic benefit is often context-specific, as the hippocampus encodes the context of extinction, and fear may be renewed in the real world
It is dependent on concurrent SSRI administration to generalise across contexts

correct_answer.text: Therapeutic benefit is often context-specific, as the hippocampus encodes the context of extinction, and fear may be renewed in the real world

questions.explanation: Because the hippocampus stores the contextual information of where extinction occurred, the therapeutic learning may be restricted to the specific context in which it was acquired — typically the therapist's office. Outside that context, in environments associated with the original trauma or fear, the original conditioning may reassert itself (renewal). Current psychotherapy research is investigating how to use contextual cues to strengthen generalisation of extinction learning across different environments.

questions.question_text: Which combination of psychosocial interventions is recommended as first-line for mild PMS?

options.text: CBT, exercise, dietary regulation, and lifestyle changes

correct_answer.text: CBT, exercise, dietary regulation, and lifestyle changes

questions.explanation: Mild symptoms can be managed by making lifestyle changes, CBT, exercise or dietary regulation. These non-pharmacological approaches are explicitly recommended as first-line for milder presentations before progressing to SSRIs or other medications.

questions.question_text: What is the primary modality of social skills training?
questions.explanation: Social skills rehabilitation can help improve social perceptions, social cognitions, and behavioral responses via focusing on role-playing of simulated conversations.

questions.question_text: Triangulation in family systems theory refers to:

options.text: Involvement of a third party to reduce tension between two members

correct_answer.text: Involvement of a third party to reduce tension between two members

questions.explanation: Triangulation occurs when tension between two family members is managed by involving a third member, often an unhealthy family dynamic.

questions.question_text: Jack has certain core beliefs about being unlovable. He thinks that this characteristic makes people abandon him. In order to avoid this, he turns out to be excessively self-sacrifi cing to his family. From a schema-based treatment point of view, what is the underlying cognitive process that is maintaining the schema?
questions.explanation: Schema-based approaches in cognitive therapy are based on the original ideas of Beck. Early life experiences produce a number of thought patterns or schemata. These thought patterns are like ‘block moulds’ into which thoughts fi t in when evaluating events. They are otherwise called core beliefs. These result in underlying ‘assumptions’ which reinforce the core beliefs and from these arise the negative automatic thoughts. Schemata are thought to be dormant, and get activated during a depressive episode. Schemata are patterns of unconditional beliefs that are hard to access and are self-maintaining. There are thought to be three main processes that maintain schemata. Schema surrender is the process where the person seeks evidence that supports the beliefs and dismisses any evidence to the contrary. Schema compensation refers to compensating for the core belief by doing the exact opposite, but, ultimately, this action acts as a reinforcer that maintains the schema, as in the case described in the question. Ultimately, the person believes that the family loves him only because he is self-sacrifi cing, and if he was not, he would still remain unlovable. Schema avoidance is a group of blocking behaviours that help avoid emotional arousal – e.g. comfort eating. Naismith J and Grant S. Seminars in the Psychotherapies. Gaskell, 2007, p. 149.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the approach that reflects on how intended outcomes are affected by current behaviours?
questions.explanation: Motivational interviewing is a counselling method that helps people resolve ambivalent feelings and insecurities to find the internal motivation they need to change their behaviour. It is a practical, empathetic, and short-term process that takes into consideration how difficult it is to make life changes.

questions.question_text: Which skill is considered the first step in effective interpersonal problem solving?
questions.explanation: Acquiring good social perception is considered the first step in effective interpersonal problem solving. Training someone to perceive and interpret social and cognitive cues can help with more specific communication and coping skills.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is a technique for automatic thought modifi cation?

options.text: Behavioral activation and scheduling of pleasant activities

questions.explanation: Examining the evidence is a technique in which the therapist and patient collaboratively explore the evidence for and the evidence against a specifi c distorted thought or belief. When working through the exercise, the therapist asks the patient to write the thought or belief at the top of a piece of paper and then label two columns with ‘evidence for’ and ‘evidence against’ the thought. The patient is then guided to explore methodically and write down each piece of evidence. At the end of this procedure, the evidence for and against the cognition is quantifi ed and estimated. Guided discovery is the most frequently used technique to help patients articulate automatic thoughts in sessions. The specifi c technique used is called Socratic questioning. One of the most powerful ways of teaching patients to detect automatic thoughts is to fi nd a real-life example of how automatic thoughts infl uence their emotional responses. A shift in mood during the therapy session can be an opportune time for the therapist to facilitate the identifi cation of automatic thoughts. The Automatic Thoughts Questionnaire devised by Hollon and Kendall is a comprehensive list of dysfunctional thoughts that has been used primarily in research studies. Similar lists can be used in clinical settings when patients are having diffi culty detecting their automatic thoughts. Imagery and role-play are two methods for uncovering cognitions when direct questions are unsuccessful (or partially successful) in generating suspected automatic thinking. Gabbard GO. Textbook of Psychotherapeutic Treatments in Psychiatry, 1st edn. American Psychiatric Publishing, 2008, p. 208. Hollon SD and Kendall PC (1980) Cognitive self-statements in depression: development of an automatic thoughts questionnaire. Cognitive Therapy and Research 4: 383–395.

questions.question_text: Rogerian therapy based on motivational interviewing is:
questions.explanation: Rogerian therapy (person-centered therapy developed by Carl Rogers) is based on humanistic principles and forms the foundation of motivational interviewing. It emphasizes unconditional positive regard, empathy, and self-actualization, contrasting with cognitive-behavioral or analytic approaches.

questions.question_text: An alcoholic patient is taken to a place with alcohol and environmental cues associated with drinking, but prevented from drinking. What therapeutic technique is this?
questions.explanation: Cue exposure therapy involves exposing the patient to cues associated with substance use while preventing the use, with the goal of extinguishing the conditioned craving response.

questions.question_text: You experience attraction to your individual during initial evaluation to the point that you have difficulty focusing on the interview. What is the next appropriate step in this situation?

options.text: Tell the individual that you are attracted to her.
Consult with the treatment team about managing countertransference appropriately.
Discuss this issue with a colleague or a supervisor.
Discharge the individual so that you can ask her out on a date.

correct_answer.text: Discuss this issue with a colleague or a supervisor.

questions.explanation: Although transferring the patient may ultimately be appropriate, it is essential to identify and discuss this issue with a colleague or a supervisor because you are having difficulty responding objectively in this situation. Telling patients about countertransference, particularly early in the course of care, is not advisable unless there is a firm therapeutic alliance and introducing this information is intended for the patient’s benefit rather than for the benefit of the physician. BIBlIOgRAPHY Sadock, B.J, & Ruiz, P. (2015). Psychiatric interview, history and mental status examination. In Kaplan and Sadock’s synopsis of psychiatry: Behavioral sciences, clinical psychiatry (11th ed., p. 194). (J.A.Sadock, Ed.). Philadelphia, PA: Wolters Kluwer.

questions.question_text: Which option most accurately characterizes countertransference?

options.text: The activation by the individual of repressed object representations within the therapist
An aspect of the individual’s self that is acknowledged and consciously projected onto the therapist
The therapist’s total emotional reaction to the individual, conscious or unconscious
A process by which only the therapist contributes to the intersubjective interpretive space between self and therapist
The internal reward a therapist gains when a individual improves

correct_answer.text: The therapist’s total emotional reaction to the individual, conscious or unconscious

questions.explanation: In psychoanalytic theory, countertransference occurs when the therapist begins to project his or her own unresolved conflicts onto the client. While transference of the client’s conflicts onto the therapist is considered a healthy and normal part of psychodynamic therapy, the therapist’s job is to remain neutral. At one time, countertransference was widely believed to contaminate the therapeutic relationship. Current thinking is more complex and suggests countertransference can play an important role when those feelings are utilized productively in the therapeutic process. ommuNiCatioN skills • 313

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is an evidencebased treatment for PTSD?
questions.explanation: Cognitive Processing Therapy and Prolonged Exposure Therapy are evidencebased psychotherapy treatments for PTSD. Cognitive Processing Therapy involves written accounts of the trauma narrative with cognitive restructuring. In Prolonged Exposure Therapy, the trauma narrative is repeated orally during the therapy, and in vivo exposures are utilized to reduce distress and avoid situations impacted by the PTSD. Fluoxetine is an SSRI antidepressant that is used to reduce symptoms of PTSD. Each of these three treatments can help PTSD symptoms related to reexperiencing (such as nightmares), avoidance (such as detachment), and hyperarousal (such as hypervigilance).

questions.question_text: Which therapy is based on the principle of reciprocal inhibition?
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitization is based on the principle of reciprocal inhibition, where an incompatible relaxation response is paired with anxiety-provoking stimuli.

questions.question_text: In treatment of personality disorders, which of the following psychotherapeutic approaches should be avoided?

options.text: Maintenance of professional distance and clear boundaries
Giving concrete advice on personal and social problems
Initial focus on the individual’s chief complaint

correct_answer.text: Giving concrete advice on personal and social problems

questions.explanation: Giving concrete advice on personal and social problems to patients with a variety of personality disorders may 28. tREatmENt oF PsyCh elicit resentment, dependence, or noncompliance with treatment. Although specific personality disorders utilize different treatment modalities, there are several general psychotherapeutic principles that can be helpful in treatment of patients with personality disorders. To establish rapport, an initial focus on the patient’s chief complaint and an emphasis on healthy lifestyle choices may be helpful, particularly if patients were “forced into treatment” by a friend or family member. Goal setting helps patients to focus the therapy and achieve a sense of accomplishment. Maintenance of professional objectivity is necessary to cope with strong feelings of countertransference.

questions.question_text: Reciprocal inhibition is the principle underlying which therapeutic technique?
questions.explanation: Reciprocal inhibition is the principle that two opposing physiological states cannot occur simultaneously. This principle is central to systematic desensitization, where relaxation (incompatible with anxiety) is paired with graduated exposure to anxiety-provoking stimuli.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which statements accurately describes collaborative empiricism in CBT?

options.text: A relationship where the therapist validates the client's beliefs without questioning them
A relationship in which the treatment is considered empirical with no guaranteed positive outcome in order to avoid later disappointment
A relationship in which the therapist discloses personal problems to the client for mutual problem-solving
A relationship in which the therapist and the client work as partners in identifying and modifying dysfunctional cognitions and behaviours.
A relationship in which the client agrees for the therapist to share information with multiple other therapists who offer different models of treatment

correct_answer.text: A relationship in which the therapist and the client work as partners in identifying and modifying dysfunctional cognitions and behaviours.

questions.explanation: Collaborative empiricism is a term used in cognitive therapy to describe the therapeutic relationship with a high degree of collaboration and an experimental but pragmatic tone to the therapy. This allows the therapist to formulate hypotheses and helps the client to test the validity of the hypotheses, thus actively contributing to the client’s therapy. It does not necessarily mean that the client and the therapist must agree with each other on every aspect of the therapy. In addition, the therapist need not collude with dysfunctional assumptions the client holds in order to achieve the collaboration. Sadock BJ and Sadock VA. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry: Behavioral Sciences/clinical Psychiatry, 10th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2007, p. 964.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is the central principle of dualsex treatment as developed by Masters and Johnson?

options.text: This shows your pattern of seeing me as untrustworthy.
You seem to be testing whether I will set appropriate boundaries.
Let's explore what this might mean in the context of your experience.

questions.explanation: Several synthetic and semisynthetic opioids are not detected on routine urine toxicology screening. For instance, fentanyl, buprenorphine, and methadone require assays for these substances in particular given structural differences relative to naturally occurring opioids (i.e., opiates), including morphine and codeine. Of note, all agents that activate mu receptors are known as opioids (literally, “resembling opiates”), and agonists that are structurally related to compounds derived from opium poppy are opiates proper. The DSM5 uses the more encompassing term opioid, as in “opioid use disorder” and “opioid withdrawal.”

questions.question_text: Cue Exposure Therapy (CET) is a behavioristic psychological approach to treating substance use disorders. What does CET involve?

options.text: Administering controlled doses of the substance to build tolerance
Exposing patients to relevant drug cues without allowing consumption to extinguish conditioned responses
Using medication to block cravings while avoiding environmental triggers
Cognitive restructuring to change beliefs about substance use
Supervised consumption in a controlled medical environment

correct_answer.text: Exposing patients to relevant drug cues without allowing consumption to extinguish conditioned responses

questions.explanation: Cue Exposure Therapy exposes alcohol-dependent patients to the sight and smell of alcohol without allowing consumption in an attempt to weaken the conditioned stimulus-unconditioned stimulus (CS-US) link via extinction and attenuate cravings.

questions.question_text: CAT - Snags, Dilemmas, Traps A therapist identifies patterns where the patient sabotages success, faces impossible choices, or gets stuck in self-reinforcing cycles. Which therapy uses these concepts?
questions.explanation: CAT (Cognitive Analytic Therapy) uses snags (self-sabotage), dilemmas (false either/or choices), and traps (self-reinforcing patterns).

questions.question_text: What would be the average number of sessions in cognitive behavioral treatment?
questions.explanation: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is usually a shortterm approach, typically with 12 to 20 sessions. CBT is a collaborative, structured, and goaloriented intervention that targets core components of a given disorder. The “cognitive” HIATRIC dISOR dERS • 85 element involves cognitive restructuring and problemsolving that addresses automatic thoughts. The “behavioral” component involves versions of monitoring, exposure, scheduling, and skills training.

questions.question_text: Cue exposure therapy for substance use disorders involves

options.text: Administration of the substance in controlled doses
Exposure to drug cues without actual substance consumption to weaken conditioned responses
Cognitive restructuring of thoughts about drugs

correct_answer.text: Exposure to drug cues without actual substance consumption to weaken conditioned responses

questions.explanation: Cue exposure therapy (CET) exposes patients to relevant drug cues (sight, smell of alcohol) without allowing consumption, attempting to weaken the conditioned stimulus-unconditioned stimulus link via extinction.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which therapies involve ‘strokes’ that people exchange and ‘games’ that people play?
questions.explanation: Transactional analysis developed by Eric Berne in 1960s. According to Berne, transactions are stimuli presented by one person that evoke a corresponding response in another. Berne defi ned psychological ‘games’ as stereotyped and predictable transactions that people learn in childhood and continue to play throughout their lives. Strokes, the basic motivating factors of human behaviour consist of specifi c rewards such as approval and love. All people have three ego states that exist within them: the child (the primitive element), the adult (the reality element), and the parent (an introject of the values of a person’s actual parents). The therapeutic process helps people to understand whether they are functioning in a child, adult or parent mode when interacting with others. It is thought that as patients learn to recognize characteristic games being repeated throughout life, they can ultimately function in the adult mode as much as possible in interpersonal relationships. Sadock BJ and Sadock VA. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry: Behavioral Sciences/clinical Psychiatry, 10th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2007, p. 216. Freeman C and Power M (). Handbook of Evidence-based Psychotherapies: A Guide for Research and Practice, 1st edn. WileyBlackwell 2007, p. 129.

questions.question_text: Identifying unspoken rules within family systems is a focus of which family therapy approach?
questions.explanation: Structural family therapy focuses on understanding and restructuring family boundaries, hierarchies, and unspoken rules that govern family functioning.

questions.question_text: You experience attraction to your individual during initial evaluation to the point that you have difficulty focusing on the interview. What is the next appropriate step in this situation?

options.text: Tell the individual that you are attracted to her.
Consult with the treatment team about managing countertransference appropriately.
Discuss this issue with a colleague or a supervisor.
Discharge the individual so that you can ask her out on a date.

correct_answer.text: Discuss this issue with a colleague or a supervisor.

questions.explanation: Although transferring the patient may ultimately be appropriate, it is essential to identify and discuss this issue with a colleague or a supervisor because you are having difficulty responding objectively in this situation. Telling patients about countertransference, particularly early in the course of care, is not advisable unless there is a firm therapeutic alliance and introducing this information is intended for the patient’s benefit rather than for the benefit of the physician. BIBlIOgRAPHY Sadock, B.J, & Ruiz, P. (2015). Psychiatric interview, history and mental status examination. In Kaplan and Sadock’s synopsis of psychiatry: Behavioral sciences, clinical psychiatry (11th ed., p. 194). (J.A.Sadock, Ed.). Philadelphia, PA: Wolters Kluwer.

questions.question_text: Which therapeutic approach involves reflecting on how intended outcomes are affected by current behaviors?
questions.explanation: Motivational interviewing is a counseling method that helps people resolve ambivalent feelings and insecurities to find internal motivation for behavior change, considering the difficulty of making life changes. It involves reflecting on discrepancies between current behaviors and desired outcomes. While Rogerian therapy uses reflection, motivational interviewing specifically focuses on exploring the gap between current behavior and intended outcomes.

questions.question_text: Caution should be used in conducting hypnosis on a patient with which of the following characteristics?
questions.explanation: Negative emotions can surface in patients with poor reality testing. As a result, caution should be used in performing hypnosis in those with paranoia, or a high need for control.

questions.question_text: Which therapeutic technique combines Rogerian client-centered therapy with Beck's cognitive behavioral therapy?
questions.explanation: Motivational interviewing integrates Rogerian person-centered techniques with cognitive-behavioral principles to enhance intrinsic motivation for change.

questions.question_text: During a biofeedback session, which of the following denotes a stage of relaxation?

options.text: Dominance of alpha waves on EEG recording
Decrease in muscle tension on electromyogram (EMG)

questions.explanation: Biofeedback is the process where certain physiological parameters of an individual are recorded and displayed. It is usually used in combination with relaxation. This involves the recording of small changes in the physiological levels (induced by relaxation) of the feedback parameter. The display can be visual or auditory. Patients are instructed to change the levels of the physiological parameter, using the feedback from the display. It is based on the idea that the autonomic nervous system can come under voluntary control through operant conditioning. The feedback instrument used depends on the patient and the specifi c problem. The most effective instruments are the electromyogram (EMG), which measures the electrical potentials of muscle fi bres; the electroencephalogram (EEG), which measures alpha waves that occur in relaxed states; the galvanic skin response (GSR) gauge, which shows decreased skin conductivity during a relaxed state; and the thermistor, which measures skin temperature (which drops during tension because of peripheral vasoconstriction). For example, in the treatment of bruxism, an EMG electrode is attached to the masseter muscle. The EMG emits a loud tone when the muscle is contracted and a low tone when at rest. Patients can learn to alter the tone to indicate relaxation. Patients receive feedback about the masseter muscle, the tone reinforces the learning, and the condition ameliorates. Sadock BJ and Sadock VA. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry: Behavioral Sciences/clinical Psychiatry, 10th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2007, p. 950.

questions.question_text: Traps, dilemmas, and snags are techniques characteristically used in
questions.explanation: Cognitive analytical therapy was fi rst developed by Ryle as a brief form of therapy. The therapy is based on the principle that purposeful behaviour activity always follows a sequence. These sequences can be faulty in three ways. Traps are repetitive cycles of behaviour in which the consequence of the behaviour perpetuates it. For example a depressed student is hopeless and stops studying for his exam. He fails the exam, and feels more hopeless and depressed. Dilemmas are false choices or unduly narrowed options. For example, people who fear angry feelings may think they have to choose between placation and aggression. They choose to placate others who then take advantage of them, thus making them even angrier. Snags are the anticipation of highly negative consequences of action such that the action is never carried out and therefore never subject to a reality check. Gelder M, Harrison P, and Cowen P. Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, 5th edn. Oxford University Press, 2006, p. 601.

questions.question_text: Exposure and response prevention (ERP) in CBT for OCD operates on the principle that:

options.text: Patients must avoid anxiety-provoking situations to reduce symptom severity
Compulsions should be gradually modified rather than immediately stopped
Patients confront anxiety-provoking situations while abstaining from compulsive responses
Relaxation training reduces the need for exposure work
Medication should be discontinued before commencing ERP

correct_answer.text: Patients confront anxiety-provoking situations while abstaining from compulsive responses

questions.explanation: ERP explicitly: Patients are trained to confront (directly or in imagination) anxiety-provoking situations while abstaining from compulsive behaviours in response. Option A represents avoidance, which is contraindicated. Option B describes graded exposure but not the abstinence from compulsions element. Options D and E represent adjunctive or contraindicated approaches not supported in the source description of ERP mechanism.

questions.question_text: Selina has had a spider phobia since she was a child. It impairs her ability to function, as she avoids any places whereby she might come across a spider: non-urban areas, public places that do not appear spotless. Her greatest fear is having a spider crawl over her face. She agrees to participate in some talking therapy to help her with her phobia. In one session, the therapist gives a very detailed description of a spider crawling across Selina's face. Her task is to withstand the anxiety until it diminishes in intensity. What method is this describing?
questions.explanation: Traditionally, in implosion, or flooding, the patient is exposed to detailed descriptions of feared situations over many hours. Gradually the times are reduced as fear diminishes for the feared situation.

questions.question_text: Group therapy is often used to treat depression and anxiety; it also has a role in personality and substance misuse disorders. Which of the following is a therapeutic aspect of group therapy?
questions.explanation: Irvin Yalom proposed a number of therapeutic factors, these include: universality, altruism, instillation of hope, imparting information, corrective recapitulation of the primary family experience, development of socializing techniques, imitative behaviour, cohesiveness, existential factors, catharsis, interpersonal learning, self-understanding.

questions.question_text: Group therapy is felt to have particular advantages over other forms of psychotherapy. Which of the following is an important advantage associated with group therapy?

options.text: It can instil hope in members of the group
The therapist can control all the interpretations made
Members of the group can imitate the therapist

correct_answer.text: It can instil hope in members of the group

questions.explanation: In a mixed group that has members at various stages of development or recovery, a member can be inspired and encouraged by another member who has overcome the problems with which they are still struggling. Group therapy is generally recognised as having more intense and rapidly expressed transference due to the multiple interactions and relationships within the group; this can be used therapeutically. The conversations can be more freeflowing and members will often interpret other's actions or beliefs. Members tend to show imitative behaviour with one another.

questions.question_text: In a behavioural technique, actual exposure to feared stimulus takes place for a substantial amount of time, so the accompanying anxiety response fades away. This is called
questions.explanation: Implosion is 'in vitro', - imaginary exposure in behavioural therapy.

questions.question_text: A patient has a phobia of escalators and avoids London tube stations as a result. Deep muscle relaxation is paired with a series of imagined scenes that are arranged in a hierarchy from the least to the most anxietyproducing stimuli. This therapy is called
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitization is a behavioral technique developed on basic principles of classical conditioning. Joseph Wolpe developed it as a means of alleviating anxiety. Deep muscle relaxation is paired with a series of imagined scenes that depict situations or objects that are associated with anxiety and thus produce anxiety. The scenes or situations are graded into a hierarchy and the pairing with relaxation proceeds from the most simple to the most severe scenes.

questions.question_text: Biofeedback can mainly modify which of the following functions?
questions.explanation: Biofeedback involves the transmission to subjects of information about biological functions. It can modify cardiovascular function and is a useful method of reducing muscle tension. It is a technique for controlling physiological responses by receiving information about these responses as they occur. Monitoring devices track physiological responses such as heart rate, blood pressure, and muscle tension and provide the person with feedback in the form of light or tone whenever they change the response in the desired direction. With practice, a person can learn to control all sorts of bodily functions predominantly through relaxation (Excerpt retrieved from http://www.abahe.co.uk/biofeedback-definition.html).
